submission.natural_language_explanation: Fires wherever the love concept is carrying the residual stream - the word love/loved/loves/loving, a cross-lingual or near-synonym equivalent (爱, 愛, 사랑, amour, 爱情, 喜欢, affection, hates, adore) - so its peaks land on the function word that continues the love phrase (' and' immediately after love, or further on the clause-opening 'I', 'would', 'do', 'people', 'much', 'a' or a comma) while the love token itself sits at about zero, and the peak grows with how much love-talk the passage carries ('Her love and devotion' peaks at 7.9 on ' and' where 'Her kindness and devotion' peaks at 1.9). Its key and value are anti-parallel: it is the most love-aligned input row in the layer (rank 1 of 4864 for ' love' in both gate_proj and up_proj, with 爱/ love/love/愛/loved/loves/Love/LOVE/loving/affection/hates as the top embedding projections) and it writes minus-love, so it removes love/Love/LOVE/loved/loves/loving/lover/lovers/爱/愛/爱情/热爱/喜爱/喜欢/爱你/사랑/amour from the next-token distribution at four times the magnitude of anything it promotes (a flat set of rare tokens) and steers the model's 'I ___' slot towards have/'m/'ve/like/think; it also rises where love is the model's own leading next-token candidate (mean p(' love') 0.091 at its >=0.25-max peaks versus 0.0002 at activation-matched controls with the same peak token, median rank 3 versus 331), which is the same love-in-the-residual quantity rather than any promotion of love.

Aside from the usual tourist spots like the Golden Gate Bridge, Alcatraz, and Fisherman's Wharf, San Francisco also offers historic architecture on nearly every corner, a serene Japanese Tea Gardens, the glorious Golden Gate Park, alongside countless cultural and artistic institutions. There’s a lot I’d like to talk about. I’ll go through every topic, insted of making the typical what went right/wrong list.

Concept

Working over the theme was probably one of the hardest tasks I had to face.

Originally, I had an idea of what kind of game I wanted to develop, gameplay wise – something with lots of enemies/actors, simple graphics, maybe set in space, controlled from a top-down view. I was confident I could fit any theme around it.

In the end, the problem with a theme like “Evolution” in a game is that evolution is unassisted. It happens through several seemingly random mutations over time, with the most apt permutation surviving. This genetic car simulator is, in my opinion, a great example of actual evolution of a species facing a challenge. But is it a game?

In a game, you need to control something to reach an objective. That control goes against what evolution is supposed to be like. If you allow the user to pick how to evolve something, it’s not evolution anymore – it’s the equivalent of intelligent design, the fable invented by creationists to combat the very idea of evolution. Being agnostic and a Pastafarian, that’s not something that rubbed me the right way.

Hence, my biggest dillema when deciding what to create was not with what I wanted to create, but with what I did not. I didn’t want to create an “intelligent design” simulator and wrongly call it evolution.

This is a problem, of course, every other contestant also had to face. And judging by the entries submitted, not many managed to work around it. I’d say the only real solution was through the use of artificial selection, somehow. So far, I haven’t seen any entry using this at its core gameplay.

Alas, this is just a fun competition and after a while I decided not to be as strict with the game idea, and allowed myself to pick whatever I thought would work out.

Alex, of Pickering, Ontario, became the fourth kid to take the job of CPO after winning a competition in 2013 organized by the Canadian division of the toy company.

Alex Thorne has held the tough job of chief play officer for Toys "R" Us Canada.

truth that singing of His love and sacrifice for us binds believers together in a way that transcends even time. No matter what melody is being sung, no matter what chords are being played by what instruments, believers have been uniting together for centuries singing about the truths of Christ's glorious death and resurrection and all that they imply. To me that's an amazing reality, and one worth giving some serious real estate in our church services!

As for the song-writing fodder I promised... this one was fun to play around with as I wrote it. I used a hemiola passage in the verse (played quietly with a wurlitzer) and bridge (a little more apparent from an electric guitar) with three notes being repeated all the way through large 4/4 phrases. I also truncated all of the phrases in the bridge--all of them 3 bars instead of four--just to add to the urgency of the concept sung there. One of the things I think is most fun, though, about this tune is that the chords in the second verse are quite different than in the first even though the melody is identical... capped off with a 2sus chord replacing the typical 5 in the first verse. Yup... theory geek stuff for sure!

By Janette Ewen

Ever since Frank Gehry’s spectacular Guggenheim Bilbao put its sleepy namesake city on the radar of architecture buffs two decades ago, design has became an integral aspect of travel and tourism, joining food, culture and climate when it comes to visitor draws. This year, the list of destinations sure to entice design fans includes spots from the West Indies to North Africa. They offer a wide range of aesthetic attractions, from cutting-edge urban design to exquisite historical gems.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
When I was nine, my grandfather cleared out half of his garage and built a workbench out of two old doors. He never called it a workshop. To him it was simply the back room, a place where the lawnmower shared space with coffee cans full of nails sorted by length, and where the smell of sawdust and machine oil hung in the air long after he had switched off the light. For three summers I stood on a milk crate beside him while he planed a board or sharpened a chisel, and he would explain, in the patient monotone of a man who had performed the same task ten thousand times, why the grain ran the way it did. I did not understand most of it. I understood that he wanted me there, and that was enough.

The house has changed hands twice since then. The garage was converted into a bedroom by a family who painted the cinderblock a pale green and hung curtains where the tool pegboard used to be. I drove past it last spring on the way to a wedding and almost did not recognise the driveway, which had been widened and paved. For a moment the old grief rose again, the way it does when a place you have carried in your head turns out to have kept none of you in return. Then I remembered how he used to wipe his hands on a rag before shaking mine, as though a boy of nine were a customer who deserved a clean greeting.

What he loved, more than the tools themselves, was the hour before dinner, when the light came in low through the side window and the radio played the ballgame and nothing had to be finished that day. He would sit on an overturned bucket with a cup of tea going cold beside him and talk about the boats he had worked on as a young man — the ferries, mostly, and one schooner whose name he could never remember without closing his eyes first. My grandmother would call from the kitchen that supper was ready, twice, three times, and he would answer each time that he was coming, and then he would go on talking.

The workbench is in my own garage now. I do not use it much, and the vice is stiff with rust, but I have not been able to throw it away. Some evenings I switch on the light out there and stand for a minute among the coffee cans, listening to the neighbours' radio through the wall, and I understand a little better what he was trying to give me.
